messages.content: Write an internal post arguing for blameless postmortems at a company that does not do them yet. Around 250 words.

**Blame is a bad way to learn things**

The checkout outage in July burned four hours. Our writeup has a "Root Cause" heading, and the sentence under it is somebody's name. A name is not a cause.

What happened was this: a config change shipped without a staging soak. The soak lives in a wiki page nobody opens, and the deploy tool doesn't check for it. Any of us would have shipped that change. Ravi was just the one holding the pager.

So let's do blameless postmortems. In practice that means no names in the document, no "should have caught it" in review comments, and a hard guarantee that whoever was closest to the incident writes the timeline and takes no hit for writing it straight.

This isn't about being nice to each other. It's about getting usable reports. People who expect to be named write less. They smooth over the twenty minutes they spent confused. They leave out the runbook that was wrong, because "I followed the runbook and it broke things" sounds worse than staying quiet. Those are exactly the parts that tell us what to fix.

Google, Etsy and Stripe all ended up here. Their engineers aren't kinder than ours; they just noticed that near-miss reports climb once reporting stops being dangerous, and near-misses cost nothing to learn from.

Give me the next three incidents. We'll run them this way and put the writeups next to the last three. If ours come out mushier or less actionable, I'll drop it and say so.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
**Blame teaches us nothing**

July's checkout outage cost us four hours. The writeup has a "Root Cause" section, and what sits under it is a person's name. A person is not a cause.

Here's the actual sequence. A config change went out without a staging soak. The soak is documented on a wiki page nobody reads, and the deploy tool never checks whether it ran. Any one of us would have shipped that change. Ravi happened to have the pager.

I want us to move to blameless postmortems. Concretely: no names in the document, no "should have caught this" in review, and a firm promise that whoever was closest to the incident writes the timeline and pays no price for writing it honestly.

This is not about being gentle with each other. It's about the quality of the report. Engineers who expect to be named write less down. They gloss over the twenty minutes they spent lost. They omit the runbook that was wrong, because "I followed the runbook and broke prod" sounds worse than silence. Those omissions are the parts we most need.

Google, Etsy and Stripe all landed here. Their engineers are no kinder than ours. They just observed that near-miss reports go up once reporting stops carrying risk, and near-misses are free lessons.

Give me the next three incidents. We'll write them this way and set them beside the last three. If ours read vaguer or turn up fewer fixes, I'll say so and drop it.
